name: Tibialis Wall Raise with Isometric Hold
description: A tibialis anterior strengthening exercise performed standing with the back against a wall and heels a short distance from the wall. The exerciser raises the toes and forefoot off the floor (dorsiflexion) and holds the top position for a prescribed duration. The isometric hold component greatly increases time-under-tension for the tibialis anterior compared to repetitive raises, making it effective for shin splint rehabilitation and tibialis anterior endurance development.

execution.starting_position: Stand with the back flat against a wall, feet approximately 30-40 cm from the wall, heels on the floor. The calves rest gently against the wall for proprioceptive feedback.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment needed. Any wall works. Ensure the floor surface is non-slip.
steps: Step 1: Stand with back against the wall, heels on the floor, feet slightly away from the wall.
Step 2: Raise both forefeet off the floor to maximum dorsiflexion — toes pointing toward the ceiling.
Step 3: Hold the dorsiflexed position for the prescribed duration (5-30 seconds), maintaining maximum height.
Step 4: Lower slowly to the floor. Rest briefly and repeat.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe continuously during the hold. Do not hold your breath.
common_mistakes: Partial dorsiflexion — not raising the toes to their full height
Pushing through the toes rather than lifting the forefoot
Leaning forward away from the wall — maintain full back-wall contact
safety_considerations: If acute shin splints are present, begin with very short holds (3-5 seconds) and progress as symptoms allow
Pain during the exercise above 3/10 suggests the load or duration should be reduced
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full dorsiflexion — toes as high as possible from the floor.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2s raise, 5-30s isometric hold, 2s lower. Begin at 5s holds and progress to 30s.
coaching_cues: Lift the toes as high as possible toward the ceiling
Feel the outer shin muscles working — that is the tibialis anterior
Keep breathing during the hold — count seconds to track duration
